To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Purdue pegboard and key pinch dynamometry were age sensitive in patients with GSD type III, while the MMT, the MFM score and the handgrip strength only in patients aged 29 years and older.
the Purdue pegboard, dynamometry of key grip pinch and knee extension are age-sensitive outcome measures in patients with glycogenesis storage disease type III.

muscle function in patients aged between 12 and 60 years with glycogen storage type III was age-sensitive, with an annual decline of 0.7 to 1.5% of the predicted value, depending on the outcome measure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of promising outcome measures to be used in future studies on natural progression and therapeutic trials in patients with glycogenesis type III.
identifying age-sensitive muscle strength measures for future clinical studies.
the development of outcome measures that are sensitive to changes in the disease course.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Purdue Pegboard Test, key pinch and knee extensor dynamometry are the most promising measures for future longitudinal studies.
muscle strength assessed by manual muscle testing and dynamometry of elbow extension strength are not promising outcome measures for clinical trials in patients with glycogenesis type III.
the most sensitive measures are Purdue pegboard, dynamometry for key pinch and knee extensors, and MFM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the MMT, the elbow extension strength measured by HHD and the MFM are not age-sensitive, but the Purdue pegboard, the knee extension, the handgrip and the key pinch strength measured by HMD are age-sensitive.
the Purdue pegboard, the knee and the key pinch dynamometry are the most promising muscle outcomes in patients with glycogenic storage disease type III.

the Purdue pegboard, the knee extension strength and the handgrip strength should be considered as promising muscle function outcomes for future clinical trials in patients with glycogenesis type III.
The main takeaway from our work is that
muscle function is age sensitive and therefore, longitudinal studies should be performed with the aim to evaluate the natural progression of disease or the effects of therapeutic interventions.
the MMT and elbow strength measured by the HHD are insensitive to the age-related changes in muscle function and thus unlikely to be useful outcome measures in future studies.
the Purdue pegboard and dynamometry for key pinch and knee extensors are age-sensitive measures in patients with GSD III.
